generally speaking.n: A sentence opener that signals a broad truth with exceptions. Speakers use it to introduce an overview before details, which makes it handy in IELTS Speaking and in essays that compare groups. It is followed by a comma and then a full clause. It is slightly more formal than usually, and it sits comfortably beside on the whole and in general. Avoid it when you mean a single, specific case, because it promises a pattern.
x: Generally speaking, trains here run on time, although winter can cause delays.
I can manage most tasks alone, but generally speaking, I prefer working in a team.

lead to.n: A phrasal verb followed by a noun or an -ing form, usually for consequences and especially in discussion essays on causes and effects. Remember that to is a preposition here, so write lead to increasing costs, not lead to increase costs. The past form is led to. It is neutral in tone and a little less direct than cause, as it often suggests a chain of events rather than one immediate result. Compare result in, which is nearly interchangeable.
x: Poor sleep can lead to mistakes at work and reduced concentration.
Rising rents may lead to more people moving away from the city centre.

over the period.n: A fixed phrase for describing trends in charts, graphs and tables. It often takes shown, covered or in question, and usually sits at the end of the clause or right after the verb: prices rose over the period shown. Compare during the period, which points to events inside a time span, and over the whole period, which stresses the full range. In Task 1 writing it is a tidy alternative to repeating dates. Avoid it when you have not yet defined the period for the reader.
x: Bus passenger numbers climbed steadily over the period covered by the survey.
Sales of printed books stayed roughly level over the period, despite the rise of e-readers.

to be honest.n: A discourse marker that introduces a frank opinion, often one the listener may not expect or want. It is often followed by a comma, as in to be honest, I was a bit disappointed. It suits speech and informal writing best; in formal academic writing prefer frankly or candidly, or simply state the view. Learners sometimes say to be honest with you that, which is not natural; end the phrase and continue. Often shortened to honestly in casual talk.
x: To be honest, I didn't enjoy the film as much as everyone else seemed to.
I would love to join you, but to be honest, I'm exhausted this week.

vocabulary.n: An uncountable noun for the words a person knows or the words used in a subject or language. Say a wide vocabulary or build up your vocabulary; do not say a vocabulary or vocabularies for general use, although a vocabulary of medical terms is possible for a specific list. Stress falls on the second syllable: vo-CAB-u-la-ry. It is not the same as a single word, so for one item use word or term. Common in study advice and IELTS lexical resource descriptions.
x: Her vocabulary is impressive for someone who started learning only two years ago.
Technical vocabulary is easier to remember when you meet it in context.

woodland.n: A noun for an area covered with trees, usually smaller or more managed than a forest, and widely used in British English for nature and countryside writing. It is normally uncountable, though woodlands appears for several separate areas. It often combines with ancient, mixed or protected, and is common in descriptions of walks and conservation. It is more neutral and slightly more scenic than woods, which is the everyday word in speech.
x: Bluebells carpet the woodland floor every spring.
The council plans to protect the remaining woodland around the village.

campsite.n: A noun for a place set aside for camping, with pitches for tents, caravans or motorhomes and usually basic facilities. It is the standard British word; American English more often says campground. It can also mean the exact spot where a group has set up camp. It is one word, though camp site occasionally appears. You book, pitch at, or arrive at a campsite, and holiday reviews often judge it by cleanliness and the shower blocks.
x: We arrived at the campsite just before dark and pitched our tent by the river.
The campsite is closed from November to March.

liberal.n: An adjective with two main uses that learners often mix up. In politics and social attitudes it means open to different views and supporting personal freedom, as in liberal values. Separately, it can mean generous, as in a liberal helping or liberal use of salt. In the United States it usually places someone on the political left, while in Europe it can point to free-market ideas, so context matters. Related noun: liberalism. Pronounced LIB-er-al or LIB-ral.
x: She grew up in a liberal household where debate was encouraged.
The chef made liberal use of garlic and fresh herbs.

licence.n: In British English licence is the noun, spelt with c, and license is the verb: you license a product, but hold a licence. American English uses license for both. The noun refers to official permission, such as a driving licence, fishing licence or a licence to broadcast. Common verbs are apply for, renew, hold and revoke a licence. Related phrase: under licence, meaning made with the owner's permission.
x: You need a valid licence to run a restaurant that serves alcohol.
The company lost its licence after repeated safety failures.

logic.n: An uncountable noun for sound reasoning, and also the formal study of valid arguments. It is common in essays when you judge whether an argument makes sense: the logic of the argument, flawed logic, follow the logic. The adjective is logical, the adverb logically. Stress is on the first syllable: LOJ-ik. It is stronger and more abstract than common sense, and suggests steps that can be checked rather than a feeling.
x: I couldn't follow the logic behind the manager's decision.
The logic of the experiment is simple: change one factor and measure the result.

manipulate.n: A verb with two quite different tones. In everyday and critical writing it usually means to control or influence people dishonestly, as in manipulate voters. In science, engineering and computing it is neutral: to handle or alter data, objects or images skilfully. The noun is manipulation and the adjective manipulative, which is always negative of a person. Choose it carefully in essays, since readers may assume a negative meaning unless the object, such as data, makes it technical.
x: Some politicians try to manipulate public opinion through selective statistics.
The software lets users manipulate images without losing quality.

margin.n: A noun with several senses. The most common is the blank space at the edge of a page. In results, votes and sports it means the amount by which something is won or lost, usually described as narrow, wide or comfortable, as in win by a narrow margin. In business, margin is profit as a share of price, as in a thin profit margin. Margin of error is used in statistics. Stress is on the first syllable: MAR-jin.
x: She wrote questions in the margin of every page of the report.
The champion won by a comfortable margin of nearly thirty seconds.

mature.n: An adjective for being fully developed, whether a person, plant, market or idea. For people it suggests sensible adult behaviour, as in a mature attitude, and the opposite is immature. Mature student refers to an adult who enters university later than usual. Use it carefully when describing age: calling someone mature can sound like a polite way of saying older. It is also a verb meaning to become fully developed, with the noun maturity.
x: For his age, he is remarkably mature and calm in a crisis.
Mature cheese develops a stronger flavour over many months.

maximise.n: A verb meaning to make something as large or as effective as possible. It is the British spelling; American English writes maximize. It is formal and common in business, economics and academic writing, usually followed by an object such as profit, efficiency or benefit. The noun is maximum, the adjective maximal is rarer. The usual opposite is minimise, and it is stronger than simply increase because it implies reaching the limit.
x: The team worked to maximise the use of natural light in the building.
Students should maximise their study time by planning each week.

military.n: An adjective relating to the armed forces, as in military service, military action or military base. It can also be a noun with the: the military, meaning the armed forces as a group, which takes a singular or plural verb. It is neutral and common in news and politics. Do not confuse it with army, which is only one branch. Collocations include military spending, military coup and military personnel. Stress is MIL-i-tar-y.
x: The government increased military spending for the third year in a row.
He joined the military straight after school and trained as a pilot.

minimal.n: An adjective meaning very small or as little as possible. It fits formal writing, for example a minimal effect on prices or minimal risk, and it is stronger than small, because it suggests the amount is almost at the lowest possible point. It also describes a style that uses few elements, as in a minimal design. It is not the same as minimum, which names a lowest amount rather than describing a degree. The adverb is minimally.
x: The repairs caused minimal disruption to local traffic.
With minimal training, most staff can use the new booking system.

minimise.n: A verb meaning to reduce something to the lowest possible level, spelt minimize in American English. It is not the same as decrease: minimise means push down as far as you can, not just make smaller. It collocates with risk and loss, as in minimise the risk of infection or minimise losses, and also with damage, waste and cost. It is formal and common in instructions and reports. In computing it also means to shrink a window.
x: Wearing a helmet can minimise the risk of serious head injury.
The airline tried to minimise delays by adding extra staff at peak times.

ministry.n: A noun for a government department headed by a minister, mainly in British and international usage, as in the Ministry of Defence. In the United States the equivalent is usually a department. It is capitalised when part of an official name, but not in general reference to the ministry's decision. It can also mean the work of a religious minister, which is a separate meaning. Plural: ministries. A person in charge is a minister, not a ministry head.
x: A spokesman for the ministry said an investigation was under way.
The ministry shares responsibility for the national road network with local councils.

minor.n: An adjective for something small or less important than others of its kind, such as a minor injury, minor role or minor repairs. The opposite is major. It differs from little, which can be only about size, because minor compares importance. As a noun it also means a person under the legal age of adulthood, a formal legal sense. In music, a minor key is a technical term. It is usually placed before a noun.
x: He suffered only minor injuries in the accident.
The actress played a minor role in the first series.

modify.n: A verb meaning to change something a little, usually to improve it or make it suitable. It is more formal than change and gentler than rebuild, because the original stays largely intact. Typical objects are plans, rules, designs and behaviour. It also appears in grammar, where an adjective modifies a noun, and in genetics: genetically modified crops. The noun is modification, and the past participle modified is common as an adjective.
x: Engineers had to modify the bridge design after the first tests.
You can modify the recipe by using brown sugar instead of white.

monitor.n: As a verb it means to watch and check something regularly over time, often with equipment, in medicine, science, finance and security. It takes a direct object: monitor a patient, monitor progress. Do not say monitor on. As a noun it is also a computer screen or a device that measures something, and a heart monitor is a medical example. The noun and verb are both stressed on the first syllable: MON-i-tor.
x: Doctors will monitor her blood pressure throughout the night.
Teachers need ways to monitor how well each student is progressing.

neutral.n: An adjective for not taking sides, as in a neutral country or a neutral observer, and for something without strong features, such as a neutral colour or tone. In chemistry it describes a substance that is neither acid nor alkali, and carbon neutral means no net carbon emissions. Impartial stresses fair judgement, while neutral stresses not taking a side, so a referee is impartial but a country stays neutral. Learners sometimes say neutrality person; use neutral for the adjective. A neutral is also a car gear.
x: Switzerland has remained neutral in international conflicts for centuries.
She chose neutral colours for the living room so it would feel calm.

norm.n: A noun for a standard or pattern that most people in a group accept as normal, especially in social science writing. It is more formal than standard practice or the usual way. Compare the norm, meaning what is typical (long commutes are the norm), with norms, meaning shared rules of behaviour (social norms, cultural norms). In mathematics a norm is also the size of a vector. The adjective is normal, and norm is not a general word for any rule.
x: In many workplaces, answering emails at night has become the norm.
Cultural norms about personal space differ widely from country to country.

notion.n: A noun meaning an idea or belief, often a general or slightly vague one that may not be fully accurate. It is typically followed by that, as in the notion that, or by of, and it often appears with reject, challenge or dismiss, which suggests a view being questioned. It is more formal than idea and slightly more critical. In British usage it can also mean a whim, as in he took a notion to travel, but this is dated.
x: Few historians accept the notion that the war was inevitable.
The notion of a perfect job has changed for younger workers.
